title: Throwing a large stoneware salad bowl
subtitle: A wide, open salad bowl in smooth stoneware at cone 6, 28 to 30 cm in diameter with a strong, trimmed foot ring
excerpt: A large salad bowl is the centrepiece of the thrown table: wide enough to toss a generous salad for four to six people, deep enough to contain the movement, and heavy enough to sit still. At 28 to 30 cm in diameter it represents a real step up in clay weight and wheel control from a mug or small bowl. The challenge is keeping the wide walls from sagging and the rim from becoming floppy as the form opens out.
sourceNotes: Large open bowl throwing pattern derived from first principles. Open-form throwing technique documented in Leach, A Potter's Book (1940, Faber) and Hamada Shoji studio accounts. V&A open-access collection for salad bowl form references.

glossaryTerms.definition: The working stage where clay holds its shape but remains damp enough to trim and work the surface
Air-dried but unfired; fragile, ready for bisque firing
The trimmed-back base ridge a finished pot sits on, giving a lifted, finished appearance

content.text: A large salad bowl serves a table and sits at the centre of it: it needs weight, a generous interior, and a profile that invites hands in to toss. This one throws from 1.8 kg of smooth stoneware and finishes at 28 to 30 cm in diameter and 12 to 14 cm deep. At this scale, throwing technique shifts: the walls are opened by
knuckling out
rather than the small-lump pinch pull, and controlling the spread of the wide rim without letting it sag is the defining intermediate skill.

A bat is not optional at this size. The bowl is too wide and too heavy to lift cleanly off the wheel head after throwing. Use a bat pinned to the wheel head and leave the bowl on the bat to dry before lifting.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need

materials.name: Mid-fire glaze, pre-mixed
materials.quantity: enough to glaze a large bowl interior and exterior

content.text: Preparation

Wedge 1.8 kg of smooth stoneware into a single cone-shaped lump. Wedging this quantity of clay by hand is tiring but important: air pockets in a large form will cause wall failures mid-throw. If you have access to a pug mill, use it. Pin the bat firmly to the wheel head. The bat pins should be fully seated: a large lump of clay on a loose bat will rock and cannot be centred. Have a generous bucket of water available, and a long sponge on a stick for reaching the deep interior of the bowl once the walls are up.
Throwing

Slam the 1.8 kg lump onto the centre of the bat firmly, then begin centring at medium speed. Large lumps need more pressure and more passes to centre than small ones. Use the weight of your body over the clay, not just arm strength. The clay must be completely centred before opening, or the wide floor will wobble badly.

Open the floor by pressing both thumbs or two fingers down the centre and pulling outward in one slow pass to a floor diameter of 180 mm. Leave 10 to 12 mm of clay at the base. A wide floor gives the bowl its generous interior capacity.
Begin
knuckling out

: place the inside knuckle against the wall about 30 mm from the base, outside hand positioned level and opposite, and press outward steadily as the wheel turns at medium speed. Move the knuckle slowly upward in one pass. This is how the wall gains height and the form begins to open.

Repeat the knuckling pass twice more. On the third pass, begin to allow the outside hand to guide the wall outward, creating the broad bowl profile. The target is a gentle, outward-curving wall that reaches a rim diameter of 280 to 300 mm at a height of 120 to 140 mm.

The wall at the rim will become thin and floppy as the bowl opens. Compress the rim frequently between passes: hold it lightly between thumb and index finger and run the rim through slowly to consolidate the clay. A floppy rim that is not compressed will tear or collapse.

Use the wooden rib against the outside wall to refine the curve and remove throwing marks. Hold the rib at the base of the curve, angled slightly inward, and draw it upward in one slow continuous stroke as the wheel turns slowly. Repeat on the inside wall with the rib held flat against the clay.

Smooth and compress the rim with the chamois leather. Check the rim diameter with calipers: it should be 280 to 300 mm. Use the needle tool to level the rim if any section has sagged. Let the bowl dry on the bat, covered loosely with plastic, to
leather-hard
before trimming.
Trimming
At
leather-hard

, invert the bowl onto the wheel head. A bowl this large requires a bat beneath it when trimming: invert it onto a clean flat bat and pin the bat to the wheel. Centre the inverted bowl carefully. The wide base makes it easier to see and correct any off-centre wobble.
Use calipers to mark a
foot ring
diameter of 160 mm on the base. A large bowl needs a wide foot ring for stability: too narrow and it rocks. Trim the foot ring 8 mm tall and 8 mm wide using the loop tool.

Clear clay from inside the foot ring to a depth that brings the interior of the base to 8 to 10 mm thick. Use the metal rib to scrape the base interior smooth after trimming. Compress the trimmed surfaces with a damp finger before removing from the wheel.

Check the exterior profile from the foot ring to the rim by eye: the curve should be continuous without a visible kink at the base where the foot ring transitions to the wall. Trim away any excess clay at the base of the outside wall with the loop tool to continue the curve cleanly.
Drying

Dry the bowl upright, right-side up, on a wire rack or raised surface so air can move under the foot ring. Wide forms are prone to base cracking if the base dries significantly faster than the walls. Cover the rim loosely with plastic while leaving the base open to the air, or invert a light cloth over the whole piece. Move to an uncovered position when the clay is firm enough that the rim no longer flexes under gentle touch. Continue drying to fully
bone-dry
before loading for bisque firing.
Bisque firing
Load the bone-dry bowl upright on a kiln shelf. Large bowls occupy significant kiln space: plan the load so the bowl sits on a full shelf with nothing placed inside it.
Bisque

fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius). Use a long, slow ramp for large pieces: 40 degrees Celsius per hour to 200 degrees Celsius to drive off all residual moisture, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Hold 10 minutes at peak. Cool slowly and do not open the kiln until below 100 degrees Celsius.
Glazing and glaze firing

Pour glaze into the bowl, swirl thoroughly to coat the entire interior, and pour out. Dip-glaze the exterior or apply by brushing in two coats. Leave the foot ring and 8 mm of the base free of glaze. For a bowl this size, dipping the exterior upside-down into a bucket of glaze is the most consistent method if your glaze bucket is large enough. Clean the foot ring carefully with a damp sponge. Glaze-fire to cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius). Use the same slow 40 degree per hour ramp to 200 degrees as the bisque to avoid thermal shock in the large form.
Care

Cone 6 stoneware is fully non-porous and food-safe with a lead-free glaze. The salad bowl is dishwasher-safe and suitable for daily kitchen use. It is not intended for oven use: thermal shock from sudden heat changes can crack a large bowl. Use it for cold or room-temperature serving only. Stoneware glazed with a food-safe mid-fire glaze is non-reactive with vinegar-based salad dressings and oils.
Variations

A set of matching nesting bowls from the same clay body pairs well with this large bowl: a 20 cm bowl from 900 g and a 15 cm bowl from 500 g. Use the same wall profile and foot ring proportions to make all three read as a family.

A shallow serving bowl at 30 cm in diameter and only 7 cm deep from the same clay weight makes a wide, dramatic pasta or salad plate. The throwing technique is the same but the final wall angle is more dramatically outward-flared, almost horizontal at the rim.

For a decorative rim treatment, use a serrated metal rib held against the outside of the rim as the wheel turns slowly to leave a regular wave pattern around the circumference. This works best when the clay is still soft from throwing, before the chamois pass.

rows.cause: Too much water used or wall thinned too quickly on a wide, heavy form
rows.fix: Use less water: dip fingers rather than pouring. Take more passes at thicker walls and thin gradually. Stop throwing if the clay becomes saturated and allow it to firm up slightly before continuing.

rows.cause: Rim not compressed between passes on a wide form
rows.fix: Compress the rim after every knuckling pass. Hold the rim between thumb and index finger gently as the wheel turns at low speed.

rows.cause: Base dried significantly faster than the walls
rows.fix: Slow the base drying by placing the bowl on a foam bat rather than a solid surface. Cover the base underside with plastic while the walls catch up in drying rate.

rows.problem: Foot ring uneven in height around the circumference
rows.cause: Bowl not centred accurately when inverted for trimming
rows.fix: Spend more time on centring the inverted bowl. Tap the base toward centre while the wheel turns slowly, and do not begin trimming until a needle held at the foot ring position shows no bounce.

rows.problem: Glaze coat uneven on the large exterior
rows.cause: Brushing applied too thin in some areas on a large surface
rows.fix: Apply by dipping where possible. If brushing, apply two coats at right angles to each other and check coverage under a bright light before loading.
